metadata.title: Adults with low literacy and numeracy skills (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This document is a literature review of policy interventions for adults with low literacy and numeracy skills and does not conduct a student-level secondary analysis of PIAAC microdata. As a result, there is no analytic sample drawn from PIAAC, no sampling frame, and no application of complex survey weights or replicate-weight variance estimation. The review synthesises findings from prior empirical studies and policy reports, including references to PIAAC as a measurement context rather than as a dataset used for estimation in this paper. For any future empirical work using PIAAC microdata, analysts should apply the PIAAC sampling weights and replicate weights provided in the Data Explorer/IDB to obtain population-representative estimates and correct standard errors under the complex survey design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are not applicable because this is not an empirical analysis of PIAAC (or another ILSA) microdata with achievement outcomes; it is a narrative literature review synthesising evidence on interventions. Missing-data handling is not reported because the paper does not estimate models on individual-level assessment records where missingness would require imputation or deletion rules. Therefore, PV and missing-data procedures are outside the scope of this document’s methodology.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Not applicable: the paper is a literature review and does not define an analytic subsample from PIAAC or any other ILSA microdata. It instead synthesises evidence from prior empirical studies and policy documents, with PIAAC referenced as the measurement context for adult literacy and numeracy levels.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper is a literature review focused on policy interventions for adults with low literacy and numeracy skills, drawing on evidence from multiple countries and programme types. It does not estimate predictive or causal models on PIAAC microdata; instead, it synthesises findings about what tends to motivate adults to join and persist, and which teaching approaches are described as promising (notably formative assessment, e-learning, and contextualised/embedded provision, especially in workplace and family settings). The review highlights that successful interventions are relatively uncommon and that evaluation evidence is often weak, with frequent limitations such as short follow-up windows and insufficient comparison groups. It also stresses that the low-skilled adult population is heterogeneous, implying that one-size-fits-all solutions are unlikely. The main policy implication is to translate emerging evidence on effective teaching and learning approaches into scalable programme design, while improving evaluation quality to better identify which levers work for which subgroups.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse with respect to sample size, country-level Ns, and ML methodology because the document is explicitly a literature review rather than an empirical large-scale assessment analysis. Consequently, there is no student-level dataset used for estimation, no PV generation/combining, and no missing-data or weighting protocol tied to an analytic model. The review’s contribution is conceptual and policy-synthetic: it aggregates prior evidence to identify promising intervention levers and common implementation challenges.
